title: Book 5 — Terpsichore, Chapter 98
paragraphs: Aristagoras sailed on ahead and came to Miletus; and then, having devised a plan from which no advantage was likely to come for the Ionians (nor indeed was he doing what he did with that in view, but in order to vex King Darius), he sent a man to Phrygia to the Paeonians who had been taken captive by Megabazus from the river Strymon, and who were living in a district and village of Phrygia apart by themselves. When the messenger came to the Paeonians, he spoke these words: “Paeonians, Aristagoras the tyrant of Miletus has sent me to offer you salvation, if you are willing to do as he says. For now all Ionia has revolted from the king, and you have an opportunity to get safely back to your own land. To reach the sea will be your concern; after that it will from that point on be ours.” The Paeonians, hearing this, welcomed the proposal most gladly, and taking their wives and children with them, began a flight to the sea—though some of them were afraid and remained where they were. Having come to the coast, the Paeonians crossed over to Chios; and when they were already in Chios, a large body of Persian horsemen arrived in their track in pursuit of the Paeonians. These, not overtaking them, sent over to Chios and demanded that the Paeonians return. The Paeonians, however, did not accept the proposal, but the Chians ferried them from Chios to Lesbos, and the Lesbians brought them to Doriscus, and from there they proceeded by land and came to Paeonia.
